future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Causal Interventions on Causal Paths: Mapping GPT-2's Reasoning From Syntax to Semantics
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based LLMs, specifically GPT-2, understand causal reasoning in natural language, and where in the model are syntactic and semantic components of reasoning processed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that GPT-2 processes causal reasoning in two stages: syntactic cues (like 'because' and 'so') are localized in the first 2-3 layers, while specific attention heads in later layers are responsible for semantic reasoning, as shown by sensitivity to nonsensical perturbations.
papers.conclusion: The model demonstrates a syntactic focus in its initial layers and shifts to semantic processing in later layers for clear-cut causal reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic knowledge, particularly attention to causal delimiters, is concentrated in the first 2-3 layers of GPT-2.
Specific attention heads in later layers (e.g., layer 11 head 2, layer 10 head 0, layer 8 head 8) show heightened sensitivity to semantic perturbations in causal sentences.
The model's processing of causal reasoning appears to follow a two-step pattern: initial syntactic detection followed by semantic analysis in deeper layers.
Activation patching reveals that perturbed tokens significantly influence predictions in earlier layers of the residual stream.
The study provides a method for linking behavioral observations of reasoning to internal model mechanisms using causal interventions.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to clear-cut, unambiguous causal sentences; ambiguity in reasoning presents a more complex challenge.
future_direction: Explore how the model adapts when faced with ambiguous or less structured reasoning tasks.
Compare findings with larger models to determine if similar patterns emerge.
papers.abstract: While interpretability research has shed light on some internal algorithms utilized by transformer-based LLMs, reasoning in natural language, with its deep contextuality and ambiguity, defies easy categorization. As a result, formulating clear and motivating questions for circuit analysis that rely on well-defined in-domain and out-of-domain examples required for causal interventions is challenging. Although significant work has investigated circuits for specific tasks, such as indirect object identification (IOI), deciphering natural language reasoning through circuits remains difficult due to its inherent complexity. In this work, we take initial steps to characterize causal reasoning in LLMs by analyzing clear-cut cause-and-effect sentences like "I opened an umbrella because it started raining," where causal interventions may be possible through carefully crafted scenarios using GPT-2 small. Our findings indicate that causal syntax is localized within the first 2-3 layers, while certain heads in later layers exhibit heightened sensitivity to nonsensical variations of causal sentences. This suggests that models may infer reasoning by (1) detecting syntactic cues and (2) isolating distinct heads in the final layers that focus on semantic relationships.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Localizing Model Behavior with Path Patching
papers.research_question: How can we localize behaviors of neural networks to a subset of components or interactions, and how can we quantitatively test hypotheses about such localization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing hypotheses that model behaviors are localized to specific sets of paths in a computational graph.
papers.conclusion: Path patching is an expressive formalism for localization claims that is both principled and sufficiently efficient to run on real models.
papers.key_findings:
The minimal explanation of induction heads is insufficient; a refined hypothesis including additional paths (e.g., from layer 0 heads to induction heads) explains more of the behavior.
Path patching can produce sparser and more precise localizations than causal tracing or zero ablation.
Head 1.5 in the studied model implements both induction and a distinct 'parroting' heuristic for repeating tokens.
Path patching attribution can identify specific inputs where a hypothesis is unfaithful, guiding iterative refinement.
papers.limitation:
Measures sufficiency rather than completeness; a set of paths with low AUE may not be the complete set of paths responsible for the behavior.
Provides no evidence about downstream tasks; low AUE does not guarantee the abstraction is useful for applications.
Makes no claims outside the tested distribution; low AUE on one dataset does not imply low AUE on a wider distribution.
Cannot reject all false hypotheses due to potential cancellation effects in metrics like difference in expected loss.
Cannot definitively prove hypotheses, as testing all possible inputs is infeasible.
Demonstrations are narrow in scope compared to the full range of behaviors exhibited by language models.
future_direction: Scaling path patching to state-of-the-art models.
Using interpretability to detect distribution shift.
Producing adversarial examples based on knowledge of model mechanisms.
Automating hypothesis search over combinations of paths.
papers.abstract: Localizing behaviors of neural networks to a subset of the network's components or a subset of interactions between components is a natural first step towards analyzing network mechanisms and possible failure modes. Existing work is often qualitative and ad-hoc, and there is no consensus on the appropriate way to evaluate localization claims. We introduce path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing a natural class of hypotheses expressing that behaviors are localized to a set of paths. We refine an explanation of induction heads, characterize a behavior of GPT-2, and open source a framework for efficiently running similar experiments.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Towards Determining How Deep Neural Models Learn to Reason
papers.research_question: Can deep neural models learn to reason (deductive reasoning) in the absence of memorization and semantic shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a recurrent neural network trained from scratch on synthetic propositional logic formulas can achieve high accuracy in classifying theorems vs. non-theorems, suggesting that deep neural models can learn reasoning strategies without relying on memorization or semantic shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: The binary classification model is an exploratory first step towards a generative transformer-based model for theorem proving, and future work will apply mechanistic interpretability to understand learned reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The RNN classifier achieves up to 99.4% accuracy on the binary classification task of determining if a propositional formula is a theorem or non-theorem.
Performance suggests the model learns reasoning strategies rather than memorizing patterns or using semantic shortcuts.
Models with more hidden units (e.g., 128) achieve higher accuracy.
papers.limitation: The authors state that with the presented results, they cannot assert that the model has actually learned logical reasoning rules, only that it performs well on accuracy metrics.
future_direction: Generalize the approach from propositional logic to first-order logic.
Develop a generative deep transformer-based model trained on proof steps, not just binary labels.
Apply mechanistic interpretability techniques, specifically feature circuits, to analyze models trained on the synthetic data.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are well known to perform poorly on tasks involving reasoning, including deductive, inductive, abductive, and spatial reasoning. This is evidenced by many existing benchmarks. While techniques such as chain-of-thought prompting and inference computation attempt to improve reasoning performance, it is necessary to assess whether large models are ultimately "memorizing" answers to the questions being used to assess their purportedly learnt reasoning capabilities. In this short paper, we describe a work in progress that aims to investigate the innate reasoning processes of large models by generating new questions that require deductive reasoning to answer. Initially, we train from scratch and then assess the ability of a recurrent deep neural model to make such a binary decision. We then discuss how our preliminary results bear on the hypothesis that some deep neural models can indeed learn to reason in the absence of memorization and semantic shortcuts, and conclude by discussing future work.

papers.title: Deeper Insights Without Updates: The Power of In-Context Learning Over Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning capture implicit patterns better than fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns in tasks, and the authors propose circuit shift theory to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning significantly outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns within specific tasks and exhibits greater adaptability in problem-solving approaches, as evidenced by notable shifts in model circuits.
papers.key_findings:
ICL achieves higher accuracy than fine-tuning on implicit pattern detection tasks across models and tasks.
ICL is more robust to misleading data and out-of-distribution data compared to fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning plateaus quickly with more data, showing diminishing returns for implicit pattern detection.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods do not show significant improvement over full-parameter fine-tuning for implicit pattern detection.
ICL induces larger circuit shifts than fine-tuning, indicating a more significant change in the model's problem-solving approach.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is constrained by the specific nature of the implicit pattern detection tasks, limited to certain domains.
Circuit Shift analysis relies on activation patching and sensitivity analysis, which require further refinement and validation across different models and tasks.
Computational resources required for fine-tuning, especially with large models, may limit the feasibility of such experiments in broader settings.
A detailed cost-benefit analysis comparing ICL and fine-tuning in terms of computational efficiency and performance is needed.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) are two prevalent methods in imbuing large language models with task-specific knowledge. It is commonly believed that fine-tuning can surpass ICL given sufficient training samples as it allows the model to adjust its internal parameters based on the data. However, this paper presents a counterintuitive finding: For tasks with implicit patterns, ICL captures these patterns significantly better than fine-tuning. We developed several datasets featuring implicit patterns, such as sequences determining answers through parity or identifying reducible terms in calculations. We then evaluated the models' understanding of these patterns under both fine-tuning and ICL across models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The results indicate that models employing ICL can quickly grasp deep patterns and significantly improve accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning, despite utilizing thousands of times more training samples than ICL, achieved only limited improvements. We also proposed circuit shift theory from a mechanistic interpretability's view to explain why ICL wins.

papers.title: Demystifying the Roles of LLM Layers in Retrieval, Knowledge, and Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the contribution of each layer to overall LLM performance under different evaluation protocols?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematically shows that depth usage in LLMs is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent, with shallow layers dominating likelihood and retrieval tasks, while middle and deeper layers are crucial for reasoning and generation.
papers.conclusion: Results show that layer contributions are highly uneven: shallow layers dominate likelihood and retrieval, while mid-to-deep layers are essential for reasoning and generation. Depth usage is inherently task-dependent, highly metric-sensitive, and strongly model-specific, highlighting the critical need for task-aware evaluation and offering practical guidance for compression and future model design.
papers.key_findings:
Under likelihood-based metrics, pruning most layers preserves performance, with only initial layers being critical; generation-based evaluation shows middle and deeper layers are indispensable for reasoning and long-range coherence.
Knowledge and retrieval are concentrated in shallow components, with removal of early layers causing sharp degradation in retrieval tasks.
Reasoning accuracy relies heavily on deeper layers and is more sensitive to ablation in middle and deep layers.
Distillation not only improves baseline accuracy but also redistributes reasoning capacity more evenly across depth, enhancing robustness under ablation.
Retrieval and reasoning abilities are localized to specific attention heads rather than being uniformly distributed.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that the deeper layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) contribute little to representation learning and can often be removed without significant performance loss. However, such claims are typically drawn from narrow evaluations and may overlook important aspects of model behavior. In this work, we present a systematic study of depth utilization across diverse dimensions, including evaluation protocols, task categories, and model architectures. Our analysis confirms that very deep layers are generally less effective than earlier ones, but their contributions vary substantially with the evaluation setting. Under likelihood-based metrics without generation, pruning most layers preserves performance, with only the initial few being critical. By contrast, generation-based evaluation uncovers indispensable roles for middle and deeper layers in enabling reasoning and maintaining long-range coherence. We further find that knowledge and retrieval are concentrated in shallow components, whereas reasoning accuracy relies heavily on deeper layers -- yet can be reshaped through distillation. These results highlight that depth usage in LLMs is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent, underscoring the need for task-, metric-, and model-aware perspectives in both interpreting and compressing large models.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: Punctuation and Predicates in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally represent and process punctuation and reasoning rules? Specifically, how essential are punctuation tokens for model performance, and how are different reasoning rules (conditional statements and universal quantification) processed across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the importance of punctuation tokens and reasoning rules in LLMs through intervention experiments, revealing model-specific differences in how punctuation is used and how different reasoning rules are processed across layers.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals model-specific differences in how punctuation and reasoning rules are processed internally, providing new insights into the computational mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For GPT-2, punctuation tokens (period and question mark) are necessary and sufficient for performance in multiple layers, but this holds less for DeepSeek and not at all for Gemma.
Information from the first sentence is transferred to the first period token in early layers for GPT-2 and DeepSeek, indicating punctuation acts as an information summarization point.
Conditional statements (if-then) are processed early in the network, with interchange intervention accuracy dropping after a few layers, suggesting the model stops processing the consequent after early layers.
Universal quantification (all-are) is revisited throughout all layers, with interchange intervention accuracy remaining constant, indicating continuous processing.
Layer swap experiments show layers are less interchangeable for conditional statements compared to universal quantification, suggesting different processing patterns for different rule types.
papers.limitation:
The necessity and sufficiency investigation is limited to punctuation tokens (period and question mark) and only for GPT-2 in isolation, not expanded to other tokens or a wider variety of models.
Intervention analysis is done at the token level per layer, lacking more fine-grained intervention and subspace analysis.
The part-of-sentence interventions make it hard to know to what extent the results apply to syntactic processing in general versus reasoning specifically.
future_direction: Expand the investigation of necessity and sufficiency to other tokens and a wider variety of models.
Conduct deeper subspace analysis with more fine-grained interventions.
Investigate swapping entire rules (e.g., 'if then' with 'if and only if then').
papers.abstract: In this paper we explore where information is collected and how it is propagated throughout layers in large language models (LLMs). We begin by examining the surprising computational importance of punctuation tokens which previous work has identified as attention sinks and memory aids. Using intervention-based techniques, we evaluate the necessity and sufficiency (for preserving model performance) of punctuation tokens across layers in GPT-2, DeepSeek, and Gemma. Our results show stark model-specific differences: for GPT-2, punctuation is both necessary and sufficient in multiple layers, while this holds far less in DeepSeek and not at all in Gemma. Extending beyond punctuation, we ask whether LLMs process different components of input (e.g., subjects, adjectives, punctuation, full sentences) by forming early static summaries reused across the network, or if the model remains sensitive to changes in these components across layers. Extending beyond punctuation, we investigate whether different reasoning rules are processed differently by LLMs. In particular, through interchange intervention and layer-swapping experiments, we find that conditional statements (if, then), and universal quantification (for all) are processed very differently. Our findings offer new insight into the internal mechanisms of punctuation usage and reasoning in LLMs and have implications for interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and what is the role of the buffer mechanism in vertical and horizontal thinking strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces the Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) to improve reasoning performance with minimal additional parameters.
papers.conclusion: Investigates vertical and horizontal thinking strategies in Transformers from the buffer mechanism perspective and proposes RMBA to enhance multi-step reasoning, significantly improving data efficiency on 7 reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers use a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains why Chain-of-Thought (horizontal thinking) significantly improves reasoning performance.
The proposed RMBA method, with only 132 additional parameters, enhances multi-step reasoning ability and improves data efficiency on 7 real datasets.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of the kernel matrix (same-token matching).
Multi-step reasoning is not simply stacking single-step reasoning; algorithms that help single-step reasoning may not help multi-step reasoning.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning problems
Extend buffer mechanism to other types of multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Zhiwei Wang, Yunji Wang, Zhongwang Zhang, Zhangchen Zhou, Hui Jin, Tianyang Hu, Jiacheng Sun, Zhenguo Li, Yaoyu Zhang, Zhi-Qin John Xu. Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025. 2025.

papers.title: Exploring and Exploiting the Inherent Efficiency within Large Reasoning Models for Self-Guided Efficiency Enhancement
papers.research_question: Can the inherent efficiency within large reasoning models be exploited to reduce overthinking and enhance reasoning efficiency without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that large reasoning models inherently possess untapped efficiency potential, and proposes two self-guided methods—Efficiency Steering (a training-free activation steering technique) and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL (a reinforcement learning framework)—that significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance.
papers.conclusion: Overthinking in large reasoning models is a controllable behavior embedded in internal representations; the proposed self-guided methods (Efficiency Steering and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL) successfully enhance reasoning efficiency without external supervision, offering practical directions for building more cost-efficient reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LRMs exhibit inherent efficiency: the shortest correct reasoning paths are often less than half the length of the longest correct ones, indicating substantial untapped efficiency potential.
Efficient and verbose reasoning paths are linearly separable in the model's representation space, with consistent positional shifts across layers and difficulty levels.
Efficiency Steering, a training-free method that injects a single vector direction derived from contrastive reasoning pairs, can controllably modulate reasoning length without compromising accuracy.
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, which uses a dynamic reward function balancing correctness and brevity, significantly reduces reasoning length while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on simpler mathematical problems (Levels 1-3) leads to efficient reasoning that transfers well to harder problems, suggesting that efficiency priors learned from simple data are effective.
papers.limitation:
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL is sensitive to optimization steps; beyond 30 steps, efficiency improves but correctness can deteriorate, indicating a trade-off that requires careful tuning.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on harder mathematical examples (Levels 4-5) does not yield as favorable efficiency outcomes as training on simpler examples, suggesting that data distribution impacts the method's effectiveness.
future_direction: Further exploration of representational properties of LLMs to build efficiency-aware alignment strategies with minimal external supervision.
Investigating curriculum-aware or simplicity-biased training strategies for self-rewarded efficiency optimization, as simpler problems may provide better efficiency outcomes at lower training cost.
Refining the capabilities that already exist within LRMs for building more efficient and accessible reasoning systems.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced language models' capabilities in complex problem-solving by emulating human-like deliberative thinking. However, these models often exhibit overthinking (i.e., the generation of unnecessarily verbose and redundant content), which hinders efficiency and inflates inference cost. In this work, we explore the representational and behavioral origins of this inefficiency, revealing that LRMs inherently possess the capacity for more concise reasoning. Empirical analyses show that correct reasoning paths vary significantly in length, and the shortest correct responses often suffice, indicating untapped efficiency potential. Exploiting these findings, we propose two lightweight methods to enhance LRM efficiency. First, we introduce Efficiency Steering, a training-free activation steering technique that modulates reasoning behavior via a single direction in the model's representation space. Second, we develop Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically balances task accuracy and brevity by rewarding concise correct solutions. Extensive experiments on seven LRM backbones across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our methods significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance. Our results highlight that reasoning efficiency can be improved by leveraging and guiding the intrinsic capabilities of existing models in a self-guided manner.

papers.title: Parrot Mind: Towards Explaining the Complex Task Reasoning of Pretrained Large Language Models with Template-Content Structure
papers.research_question: How can pretrained large language models learn to solve complex reasoning tasks with limited training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the template-content structure (T-C structure) as an intrinsic constraint in language that reduces the learning space from exponential to linear, explaining how LLMs can generalize on complex reasoning tasks with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The template-content structure provides a plausible explanation for how LLMs acquire complex reasoning abilities through language modeling, and empirical evidence supports its existence in current models.
papers.key_findings:
The T-C structure exists in current LLMs, as evidenced by lower variance in template token outputs compared to content tokens.
The T-C structure reduces the hypothesis space from exponential to linear, enabling within-task generalization.
Hierarchical T-C structure further reduces the space to logarithmic, enabling task composition across sub-tasks.
Larger models exhibit clearer T-C structure, with higher AUC in classifying template vs. content tokens.
The T-C structure explains how LLMs can perform reasoning through language modeling (parroting) by learning and reusing templates.
papers.limitation:
The T-C structure may not hold for all tasks, such as purely natural language tasks like translation or chatting.
The assumption of token-wise alignment is a simplification; semantic alignment is more realistic but introduces challenges.
The framework assumes deterministic generation, while practical models output probability distributions and use sampling.
future_direction: Extending the framework to handle sampling and probability distributions.
Investigating the disentanglement of semantic and position information in Transformers.
Applying the T-C structure to more complex tasks and real-world scenarios.
papers.abstract: The pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown their extraordinary capacity to solve reasoning tasks, even on tasks that require a complex process involving multiple sub-steps. However, given the vast possible generation space of all the tasks, how the pretrained model learns the reasoning ability remains an open question. We firstly propose that an intrinsic structural constraint on the generated sequence of language-based reasoning -- we called it template-content structure (T-C structure) -- is the key to explain why LLMs can solve a large number of complex reasoning problems with limited training data by showing this structure can reduce the possible space from exponential level to linear level. Furthermore, by generalizing this structure to the hierarchical case, we demonstrate that models can achieve task composition, further reducing the space needed to learn from linear to logarithmic, thereby effectively learning on complex reasoning involving multiple steps. We provide both examples and formal theory of our T-C structure. We also experimentally validate the existence of the T-C structure in some current LLMs and its effectiveness for reasoning.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: Hierarchical Deconstruction of LLM Reasoning: A Graph-Based Framework for Analyzing Knowledge Utilization
papers.research_question: How do large language models use their knowledge for reasoning when solving complex real-world questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a graph-based framework to deconstruct questions by knowledge depth, introduces the DEPTH QA dataset, and analyzes forward and backward reasoning discrepancies in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: This work enhances our understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests ways to improve their problem-solving abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models exhibit larger forward and backward discrepancies compared to larger models.
Forward discrepancy occurs more frequently but with lower intensity, while backward discrepancy is less common but with higher intensity.
Memorization analysis shows that questions with lower memorization scores have higher discrepancies.
Multi-turn interactions that guide models from simpler to complex questions improve performance across model sizes.
Distinct patterns of discrepancies are observed across model capacities and memorization possibilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the advances in large language models (LLMs), how they use their knowledge for reasoning is not yet well understood. In this study, we propose a method that deconstructs complex real-world questions into a graph, representing each question as a node with predecessors of background knowledge needed to solve the question. We develop the DepthQA dataset, deconstructing questions into three depths: (i) recalling conceptual knowledge, (ii) applying procedural knowledge, and (iii) analyzing strategic knowledge. Based on a hierarchical graph, we quantify forward discrepancy, a discrepancy in LLM performance on simpler sub-problems versus complex questions. We also measure backward discrepancy where LLMs answer complex questions but struggle with simpler ones. Our analysis shows that smaller models exhibit more discrepancies than larger models. Distinct patterns of discrepancies are observed across model capacity and possibility of training data memorization. Additionally, guiding models from simpler to complex questions through multi-turn interactions improves performance across model sizes, highlighting the importance of structured intermediate steps in knowledge reasoning. This work enhances our understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests ways to improve their problem-solving abilities.

papers.title: On the Reasoning Capacity of AI Models and How to Quantify It
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the reasoning capacity of AI models, specifically how to quantify and distinguish between genuine reasoning and other cognitive processes like memorization and guessing in large language models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a phenomenological framework that decomposes model behavior into reasoning, memorization, and guessing components, showing that accuracy alone often overstates reasoning abilities and that models rely on sophisticated combinations of memorization and pattern matching.
